speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Committee was asked to look at (a) amendments arising from the constitutional amendments that we passed last year; and (b) updates to the Standing Orders more generally.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the process, the Committee considered submissions made by Mr Louis Ng and Mr Kok Heng Leun and accepted them where appropriate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I would also like to thank you, Mdm Speaker, for presiding over the Committee's deliberations with your usual fairness and efficiency.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government agrees with the recommendations of the Committee and commends them to the House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In my speech today, I will first take the House through the key recommendations made by the Committee; and, second, respond to some of the issues that were raised to the Committee.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Committee made two key recommendations arising from the constitutional amendments that we passed last year.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Such measures include Supply Bills and resolutions on certain guarantees and loans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The recommendation is for the Clerk to publish a notice in the Hansard and the Gazette if the President does not signify his decision on such measures within the prescribed time limit.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Under the Constitution, if the President fails to make a decision within the prescribed time limit, he is deemed to have agreed with the proposed measure.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Committee has recommended that procedural machinery be put in place for this purpose.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The procedures will provide that (a) the President's grounds and the CPA's recommendation must be made available two clear days before a Motion to overrule the President can be moved; (b) the Speaker must be satisfied that the President's veto was, in fact, contrary to the CPA's recommendation, as required by the Constitution; and (c) there is to be a standard form of words for Motions to overrule the President.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Committee also made a number of recommendations relating to Bill procedure.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A clear day is basically a full working day.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The increased notice applies to both Government and backbench amendments and will give Members more time to consider amendments.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, the minimum interval between the First and Second Reading of a Bill should be increased from seven clear days to 10 clear days.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In effect, this means at least two weeks must pass between the First and Second Reading of a Bill.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The increased interval would avoid situations where Bills come up for Second Reading too quickly because the House is sitting for an extended period, for example, during the Budget Debates.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In practice, the interval between First and Second Readings would generally be longer − Bills introduced are generally debated only at the next month's Sitting.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, the Second Reading of Supply Bills can be taken immediately after the end of Committee of Supply (COS) proceedings, even if the usual interval between the First and Second Reading have not elapsed.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The heads of expenditure in a Supply Bill would have been fully debated by the House during the COS proceedings, and it makes more sense for the House to go to the Second Reading immediately after COS proceedings are completed, instead of diverting to some other business, or adjourning the Sitting and coming back to the Supply Bill later.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On petitions, the Committee recommended that Parliament should be able to consider a Petition together with a Motion or Bill.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This would avoid a situation where a Petition on a Bill or Motion is still being considered by the Public Petitions Committee even though the Bill or Motion has already been dealt with by Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Committee also made a number of miscellaneous recommendations to improve Parliamentary procedure.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, a Member whose question has not been answered during Question Time should indicate within one hour after Question Time whether he wishes to postpone his question.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is to facilitate the work of the Clerks, who have to circulate written answers to Members who choose not to postpone their questions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, a Member should be able to record an abstention in a voice vote.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Currently, the Standing Orders only permit dissents to be recorded in the Votes and Proceedings.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, there should be a procedure for officeholders to correct any factual errors they make in a Parliamentary speech.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The correction would be made by a written statement circulated to Members and published in the Hansard.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Speaker's leave must be sought within 72 hours after the draft Hansard is circulated.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This procedure would ensure that factual errors on important policies and legislation in a speech are swiftly corrected, instead of having to wait until the next available Sitting to make an explanation.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Fourth, the Speaker should be able to order reprints of the Standing Orders.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The powers she would have in this regard are similar to those exercised by the Law Revision Commissioners for statute law.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many parts of the Standing Orders are drafted in very archaic styles and would benefit from some revision.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Of course, a reprint cannot make substantive changes to the Standing Orders.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Such changes would still have to be approved by Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Committee also received feedback and suggestions from Mr Louis Ng and Mr Kok Heng Leun.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It was suggested that Government Bills should be introduced together with Ministerial Statements providing key information on the Bill.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On this specific suggestion, the Committee did not think it was necessary.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If a Bill is introduced with a Ministerial Statement, any clarifications that may be sought by Members on the Ministerial Statement and the Minister's subsequent responses may pre-empt the Second Reading debate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is better that all the speeches and arguments be kept to the Second Reading debate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But I appreciate the broader point that Members need information on Bills.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Every Bill comes with an Explanatory Statement, which will provide information on what the provisions do and the broad purposes of the Bill.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To some extent, the statement is technical in nature, because it has to explain the legal provisions accurately.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But as far as possible, the Attorney-General's Chamber (AGC) will draft the statement in plain English and in an accessible way.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I encourage Members to read the statement for more information on the Bill.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A soft copy of the tracked changes will be made available on the Members' portal.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The authoritative version of the Bill will still be in today's format, but the tracked changes should make things simpler for Members who wish to go into the legislative detail.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: AGC will review the usefulness of this facility before making it a permanent arrangement.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Beyond the Bill itself, the general practice of Ministries is to release a press statement or fact sheet, which will contain more information about the policy background to the Bill.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And, at the end of the day, if a Member needs more information on a Bill that has been introduced, he or she can approach the relevant officeholder, before the Second Reading debate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I know my colleagues on the front bench will be happy to engage any Member before the debate to hear their concerns.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Standing Orders Committee was also asked to consider having Standing Select Committees to consider specific issues.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These avenues are accessible to Government, Opposition and Nominated Members alike.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, instead of looking at having new procedures and formats, I would suggest that Members make full use of the existing procedures.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If Members need any advice on the procedures, they can approach the Clerks.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We increased Question Time back in 2004, from one hour to one and a half hours.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At times, the one and a half hours are sufficient to finish all the Questions for Oral Answer.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At other times, I recognise we were not able to do so.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But there are only so many hours in a Sitting day, and we need to strike a balance between Question Time and the other demands on Parliamentary time.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: There are already instances where the House has to sit late into the night to give Members time to debate Bills and Motions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, at this point, I do not think it is right to have a permanent increase in the length of Question Time stipulated in the Standing Orders.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members will recall that Parliament increased Question Time to two and a half hours last July and last October on my Motion.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government is prepared to continue to take this approach, having regard to the number of questions and the other demands on Parliamentary time.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In appropriate cases, Ministers will also make statements to the House on important issues outside of Question Time, and Members can seek clarifications on these issues.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This was done, for example, during the Zika outbreak last year.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I should also remind Members that, if a Member's question is not reached by the end of Question Time, he can choose to postpone his question and request for an Oral Answer to be given at the next Sitting.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Otherwise, the Member will still receive a written answer to his question.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All questions filed by Members will be answered by the relevant Ministries either in oral or written form.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By way of conclusion, I should like to touch on time management in the House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I asked the Clerk to collate some statistics.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are now sitting longer hours for each Sitting.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The average for the 12th Parliament was five hours and 40 minutes.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Last month, Members would recall that we sat until 10.00 pm on 4 April.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These increases and the absolute numbers are not, in themselves, a matter of serious concern.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have more Members now, and more complex issues facing the country.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is natural that we have been sitting longer.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To some extent, we can sit longer if need be and, in fact, I would tell the House that the length of Sittings is likely to continue to increase.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But in overall terms, I would prefer to have a focused, meaningful Sitting for a few days every month.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I think this would be more beneficial for the quality of debate in the House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, I urge all Members − participate vigorously in debates by all means, but keep your speeches short, sharp and to the point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I seek some clarity on Standing Order No 54(4) which is to be deleted by way of these amendments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even though the Constitution in Article 57(1) is silent on the specific number of majority votes required, in effect, the deletion of this Standing Order supports the presence of fewer Members in the House at the closure of debate when the question is put to Members.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going back to the illustrated example, should Standing Order 54(4) remain, the same Motion would require at least eight more Members in the House, and that is assuming they intend to vote in favour of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, some members of the public may draw an adverse inference on these amendments and there may be some risk that it will reduce public trust in the institution of Parliament as Singaporeans would expect most legislators to be present in the House at any point in time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is notwithstanding the fact that Article 56 of the Constitution requires a quorum of one-quarter of Members to be present when the House is in session, failing which, Parliament shall be adjourned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be helpful if the Leader can revisit the spirit and purpose of the deleted Standing Order 54(4) in the first place and why it is this Standing Order was drafted in the first place, so as to pre-empt any adverse public opinion on this matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to get some assurance from the Leader that that ought not to happen in future, provided the list of questions the Government has can be reordered somewhat.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This relates to the change of Standing Order 18 on petitions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In gist, my concern is that the new power to be given to the House must be used with great care and should never be seen to curtail the public petition process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This might be done if the Speaker is of the view that the subject matter of the petition relates to a matter being already before the House, by a way of a Bill or Motion, in which case, the petition can be considered at the same time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Committee's report states that this is to avoid the situation where the Bill or Motion has already disposed of the matter before the PPC considers the petition, making the petition moot.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the current Standing Orders, all petitions initiated by the public must be brought to this House through a Member who is not a signatory to the petition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, the Member is not necessarily a person who shares the concerns of the petitioners but is merely a necessary conduit through which a petition may be presented to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some may ask what difference a reference to the PPC will make, since the contents of the petition can be read by Members during a debate on a related Bill or Motion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PPC is a Standing Select Committee whose procedures are governed by Standing Order 103.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Compared with the procedures of the whole House, the PPC would have more time to fully investigate the grievances of the petitioners and hear them out personally if needed, and call for relevant documents, including documents from the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The public petition procedure is provided for by the Standing Orders, and it is a vital link between Parliament and the members of the public.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a due process that should be granted to petitioners.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the petition is not referred to the PPC but is considered by the whole House during a debate of the Motion or Bill, the burden would naturally shift to the Member presenting the petition to fully convey the petitioners' concerns and grievances, which is probably expecting too much of the Member.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A petition of the Bill was presented through Nominated Member Kok Heng Leun but it was dealt with summarily during the debate of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that case, the wording of the Bill was not made public until after it was presented in Parliament for First Reading.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, it could well be said that the petitioners could not have initiated their petition any earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that debate, Nominated Member Mr Kok Heng Leun indicated his consent to have the petition heard together with the Bill and his view that this was appropriate, should be given due weight.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the House should be mindful that in future cases, we should endeavour to ensure that all petitions are granted their due process and hearing by PPC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The House should bear in mind that it may be in the public interest instead to do the opposite to defer the Motion or Bill, unless there is urgency, until the petition has been considered by PPC and its report sent to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Parliament might well benefit from a fuller understanding of the issue from the aggrieved or concerned persons before considering the Bill or Motion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With your leadership, our Parliament proceedings are smooth and efficient, and Members can debate productively and robustly while adhering to strict time limits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This report proposes several enhancements to various aspects of the Parliamentary proceedings and conduct.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are several issues which I would like to raise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the proposed amendments on the Elected Presidency, which are consequential to the constitutional amendments proposed last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I look forward to the proposed tracking of changes to amendment Bills as this will help Members while going through the various versions of the amendments and keep track of the evolution process of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the issue of petitions, I agree that it will be beneficial for the Parliament to have the option of considering a petition together with a related Bill or a Motion, instead of sending the petition to the Public Petitions Committee.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is so that Parliament can have the benefit of considering the petition while debating the Bill or Motion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Members can then scrutinise the issues raised in the petition and a full debate can occur.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When it comes to Question Time, I speak on behalf of backbenchers that we would naturally prefer more time rather than less.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it also means that if Question Time is increased, the time spent on other matters. such as debating Bills and Motions, will have to moderate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I recognise that the Government is meeting backbenchers midway by increasing Question Time on an ad hoc basis and I hope that this can be done whenever the volume of business permits or an issue is of broad public interest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I also hope that Ministers will continue and perhaps also expand on the practice of making Ministerial Statements on significant issues of broad public interest to the House, in the spirit of accountability to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will also give Members another avenue to ask questions on important issues and engage the Ministers on these issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This shows that the Government respects the important role that Members play in scrutinising and debating Government policy and proposed legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I understand that there are now no limits on how long Members can speak on each item of business and how long each item can be debated but, at the same time, it would not be prudent to prolong debates just because we can.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is ultimately the quality, rather than the length of the debate that matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A search online showed that the longest Parliament session in a single Sitting was in 1881 in the United Kingdom which lasted for 41.5 hours.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Just last year, the Australian Senate sat for 28 hours before passing a Voting Reform Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is one record that we might do well to avoid.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For us to achieve a balanced state where important matters are sufficiently debated, I hope all sides of the House will practice self-discipline, including myself, and keep our speeches short and succinct.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, I would like to make three broad points.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The debate today is not about the Constitutional amendments to the Elected President (EP).

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We had hearings and the report by the Constitutional Commission, a White Paper in Parliament, and a full debate in Parliament last November.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Opposition made its points and the Government responded.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, in amending the Standing Orders, we are refining a system that has worked well for Parliament, amended and adjusted over time to keep its relevance and effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, the amendments we are debating today were unanimously agreed by the Standing Orders Committee, with both Government and Opposition Members on it.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members were also invited to make submissions to the Committee and had one month to do so.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Committee gave a considered response to the submissions by Mr Louis Ng and Mr Kok Heng Leun.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, I would like to refer to Mr Pritam Singh who raised the issue about sequence of Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There is no rocket science involved in the sequencing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If there are a lot of questions on the topic, they get put in front.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If a question concerns a topical issue, it gets put in front.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: A balance is struck between questions from all sides of the House.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The sequence of the questions on the Order Paper is decided by the Speaker.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I give my views as the Leader of the House, but the Speaker has the final say.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The requirement was laid down in colonial times.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I asked the same question but we could not trace the real background.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it must have been around for a long time and this is really a housekeeping amendment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And that, by percentage, a quarter is more flexible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It reflects the changing number of Members in the House and, therefore, would be more relevant going forward.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Sylvia Lim raised some concerns about the move to include in the Standing Order a Motion to consider petitions together with its related Bill or Motion.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If it is carried, the petition is considered by the House.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Otherwise, the petition goes to the Public Petitions Committee.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, there is no need for a separate debate.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In any case, I take Ms Sylvia Lim's point that as much as possible − and I am sure I speak for all my frontbench colleagues − we would like to consider all viewpoints brought to the attention of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But as Members can appreciate, there are two parallel processes that are going on.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Any petition could come in on the very day that we are having a debate on a Motion or Bill and it would be advantageous if we would have the ability to consider that petition together with the Motion or Bill, as what we have done with Nominated Member Mr Kok Heng Leun's petition.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This would allow us the flexibility of including the facts and the views presented in the petition while not delaying the process that has already been ongoing for the Bill or Motion.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If the House feels strongly that a petition has to be considered separately by the Petitions Committee, they can always say no to this procedural Motion.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, it is important to the Government that we spend time in the House to explain the laws and policies that we propose.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The cut and thrust of Parliamentary debate inform the public on the important issues of the day.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Accounting to Parliament is something that the Government takes seriously.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Prime Minister's open letter to Government Members of Parliament after the 2015 General Election underscored this.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, within the House, it is important that we strike a good balance between the different demands on Parliamentary time.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Time spent on one item of business means time lost to another.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Good time management means we do not have to cut off debate.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Good time management means we have time to debate backbenchers' Motions like we did last month.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Good time management means we can have more Question Time if need be.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Good time management does not mean that Members should pull their punches or mute their criticisms of Government policy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But it does require Members to focus and deliver their key points succinctly and sharply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If anything, a succinct point is more likely to be more impactful and newsworthy than a meandering speech.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, we also need to balance the other demands on Members' time.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members know full well that a good debate in the House needs hours of preparation and homework outside.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members also need to remain in touch with different segments of society so that their arguments in the House are grounded in reality.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Elected Members need to hear the concerns of the constituents.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ministers need to run their Ministries and formulate policies.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the end of the day, after everything is said, we must make a decision and carry on.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I do not wish to see this House moving towards that state.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In this regard, I agree with Mr Desmond Choo's point that this is something that requires Members on all sides of the House to do their part.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: On policy and politics, we may well disagree and disagree sharply.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: A clarification for the Leader of the House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I appreciate very much her confirmation that when the House and, indeed, the Government debates any issue, it is important to look at all relevant viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Leader mentioned earlier that depending on the number of Questions and the amount of business for the day, these are the criteria used to extend Question Time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Say, if there are more than 80 Parliamentary Questions (PQs) or less than three Bills, then Question Time will be extended?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We run the risk at times, as we have seen in the last Sitting on 4 April, the Sitting had had to be extended to 10.00 pm.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it is not something that we could envisage in advance or with some scientific formula.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If we find that there are Questions being piled up and if the rest of the agenda allows us to do so, we will definitely extend the Question Time, as I have done so twice last year.
